item.title: Trump Announces $500 Rebates for Some Obamacare Customers, Weeks Before the Election
item.description:
The Trump administration said on Thursday that it planned to issue $500 in rebates to nearly one million people insured under the Affordable Care Act, describing the money as payments for “overcharges” by the previous administration.

People in 30 states who signed up for Obamacare insurance on heathcare.gov and did not receive a federal subsidy would be eligible, according to a White House fact sheet. The checks are scheduled to be sent next month, just weeks before the midterm elections.

The $500 checks would benefit consumers who faced significant price increases this year, after the Republican-controlled Congress did not extend more generous subsidies, or tax credits, that were approved during the coronavirus pandemic.

Many farmers, ranchers, entrepreneurs and early retirees, people who earn more than around $65,000 a year and do not get health coverage from their jobs, could receive the money.

President Trump and congressional Republicans have faced criticism from Democrats over the rising costs of health care, part of a broader critique that the administration’s policies have made everyday life less affordable.

For weeks last year, Democrats in Congress refused to vote for government spending bills unless Republicans extended the insurance subsidies, a standoff that led to a record-long government shutdown. While Democrats ultimately relented, the extended fight highlighted the political disputes over how to stem rising insurance costs.

The fact sheet posted to the White House website indicated the checks were aimed at Americans who Trump officials claimed were “most exposed” to higher Obamacare costs during the Biden administration.

“American households buying health insurance through the Obamacare exchange, which is a disaster, and the healthcare.gov were massively overcharged” by the Biden administration, President Trump said in a video posted on X. He attributed as much as $500 million to what he termed excess fees, saying they should be returned to people buying overpriced A.C.A. plans.

The Biden administration did collect more in fees than it used to operate the marketplace, but the fees were not a major source of this year’s price increases, said Larry Levitt, an executive with KFF, the health research group.

“The Biden administration actually lowered the A.C.A. marketplace user fees,” Mr. Levitt said in an email. He added that some of the available funds were intended for advertising and organizations that help people sign up for coverage, but had not been spent by the Trump administration.

The typical cost of health insurance for the population eligible for the checks increased by thousands of dollars this year, a shift that priced some out of insurance altogether and forced others to buy less generous coverage with much higher out-of-pocket costs.

The $500 rebate would make a small dent in that price increase. The checks will not go to customers in every state. Consumers in California, Colorado, Connecticut, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Washington, D.C., will get no money. Those states manage their own insurance marketplaces, and insurers there do not pay fees to the federal government.

The expiration of the extra subsidies also increased insurance costs for people with lower incomes who buy their own insurance. They will not benefit from this policy. Nor will the roughly three million who dropped Obamacare coverage once the subsidies expired.

The president is fond of sending direct payments to American voters. In his first administration, the government sent checks to taxpayers as a form of relief during the Covid-19 pandemic. Just before the 2020 election, he proposed sending $200 vouchers to Medicare beneficiaries to lower their drug costs, a plan that was abandoned.

In a speech on Wednesday, he proposed mailing $5,000 to American households next year if Republicans retain their congressional majorities. But he did not mention the Obamacare rebate. The plan was reported earlier by Axios.

Though administration officials described the checks as refunds to consumers, it will return a disproportionate share of the fees to people with incomes of more than four times the federal poverty level, or around $65,000 for a single person. The $500 total represents more money than any excess fees those customers personally paid as part of their premiums.

The White House described the checks as a one-time refund of the user fees that were not intended to be repeated next year. So far, the administration has not released an executive order or regulation establishing the rebate program outlined in the fact sheet.

But premiums in the marketplaces are on track to keep rising. Insurers have asked state regulators to increase prices by an average of about 15 percent next year, according to an analysis from KFF, though those rates are not yet final. The higher income group that may get checks will be exposed to the full brunt of those rising prices.

White House officials said they had the legal authority to use the money as they saw fit. It was collected from insurers to help operate the marketplace, but not all of it was needed. Because the user fees affected insurance premiums, the officials said it was appropriate to return the money to consumers who paid those premiums without the benefit of federal assistance.

Government health officials have “sole discretion on how user fees are set and collected for marketplace operations,” said Chris Bond, a spokesman for AHIP, an industry trade group, in a statement. “Health plans support steps to reduce underlying costs and maintain stability for those who depend on the individual market.”

The Biden administration had also sought to reroute some of this money, to help pay for contraceptive coverage.

item.title: Crashing a Plane for Clicks: Influencers Push Shock Content to Get Views
item.description:
In 2021, Trevor Jacob, a former U.S. Olympic snowboarder, flew a 1940 Taylorcraft plane far above the hills of Los Padres National Forest in Southern California and made a decision he would spend years wishing he could undo.

Cameras he had mounted to record his flight for an online audience captured him announcing that the plane had engine trouble before he bailed out.

A camera attached to a selfie stick he held recorded him parachuting safely to the ground, while cameras fixed to the plane captured it slamming into a hillside.

He posted a 13-minute video on YouTube titled “I Crashed My Plane,” which amassed some five million views. As it turned out, it was a confession.

Federal investigators later determined that the plane had never malfunctioned: Mr. Jacob had staged the crash, hoping for online fame.

The attention was fleeting.

The stunt eroded his life and led to a federal prison sentence.

Mr. Jacob is among a growing number of social media influencers who push the boundaries of safety and good taste in the quest for views, experts said.

Influencers, sensing that the algorithms reward extreme content over routine videos, are navigating this landscape, one where outrage, fear and awe hold viewers’ attention a little longer than tamer fare.

Gone are the years when internet fame was within reach for a teenager filming dance routines in a bedroom, or a parent teaching recipes from a kitchen.

Attention is currency, and sometimes it’s costly.

Across the world, aspiring influencers trespass on skyscraper roofs. They block highway traffic. They provoke strangers in grocery stores, airports and malls. They dangle from helicopters, cranes, trains and cliffs for clips lasting only seconds.

Some are arrested. Others are hospitalized. And, in tragic cases, some have died.

Psychologists who study this field are not surprised.

“As the tech has evolved and influencers stand to earn fame and wealth, it is probably not surprising that some people are willing to risk prison or even death,” said Kaveri Subrahmanyam, a psychologist at California State University.

That bet — fame and wealth weighed against the risk of prison or worse — is one that Dalton Eatherly appears to have made.

To his thousands of followers he’s known as Chud the Builder. A self-described “America-first” influencer, he has garnered views by livestreaming confrontations with Black people, which often included racial slurs and harassment.

In May, one of Mr. Eatherly’s confrontational pursuits for clicks almost proved fatal.

A dispute with a man outside the Montgomery County Courthouse in Clarksville, Tenn., ended with gunfire as both men wielded firearms.

A video later surfaced of Mr. Eatherly on a stretcher with a microphone attached to his lapel.

Mr. Eatherly claimed self-defense but was later charged with several counts, including attempted murder. The case remains pending.

He and his lawyer could not be immediately reached for comment.

The social media platforms TikTok, Kick and YouTube (which is owned by Google’s parent company, Alphabet) and Facebook and Instagram (which are owned by Meta) said that they enforce community guidelines meant to restrict objectionable and dangerous content and that they ban users who violate their policies.

“To prevent copycat behavior, we prohibit people from facilitating, organizing, or promoting harmful activities,” a Meta representative said in a statement.

Experts who have studied digital behavior and online incentives said that boundary-pushing stunts are unlikely to ease as long as social media platforms reward such content.

“In many cases, that means escalating toward ever more extreme claims and risky behaviors that can endanger not only creators themselves but also their audiences, for whom it’s increasingly difficult to distinguish between what’s truly beneficial and what may be outright harmful,” said Jasmina Tacheva, an assistant professor at the School of Information Studies at Syracuse University.

Mr. Eatherly is not the only influencer to have courted danger.

In Loudoun County, Va., Sheriff Mike Chapman’s department responded to a call involving Tanner Cook, a YouTuber behind a channel called Classified Goons.

Mr. Cook, who is known for harassing unsuspecting strangers, repeatedly confronted a DoorDash driver inside the Dulles Town Center in Sterling, Va.

Mr. Cook shoved a phone into the driver’s face while a vulgar phrase played in a loop in what was an escalation of confrontational stunts he has filmed in other places.

The driver, Alan Colie, shot Mr. Cook, who survived.

A jury acquitted Mr. Colie of aggravated malicious wounding, finding that he acted in self-defense, but convicted him of discharging a firearm inside an occupied building.

After the verdict, Mr. Cook said the shooting would not change his approach.

“We are going to continue the videos and keep it pushing,” said Mr. Cook, whose YouTube channel has 66,000 subscribers. “It is what it is.”

Recent uploads show him streaming inside stores, falsely accusing a stranger of stealing and of him being thrown out of businesses. A video posted in early 2026 is titled “I almost got shot again!”

Mr. Cook and Mr. Colie did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Sheriff Chapman’s office regularly warns residents about viral challenges and online trends. The pursuit of a laugh, he said, can carry real-world consequences.

“You may think this is funny,” Sheriff Chapman warned, “but this could end up as a disaster.”

The trend stretches beyond the United States.

The British government recently called on social media companies to remove more dangerous content, including videos of users filming themselves driving dangerously, after a string of deadly crashes that were linked to online stunts.

A press officer for Ofcom, the government’s regulator of communications services, said it opened an investigation into TikTok’s compliance with its child-safety responsibilities in July.

“Online content which encourages dangerous behavior and treats it as entertainment is totally unacceptable, and can have tragic and heartbreaking consequences,” the official said in a statement.

A TikTok representative said content that promotes dangerous behavior or could lead to serious injury violates its community guidelines, which prohibit criminal behavior, hate speech, and physical or sexual abuse, among other categories.

The platform has been redirecting videos of dangerous challenges to a safety center page. Violators can also be permanently banned, the representative said.

In France, Raphaël Graven, an internet personality who routinely subjected himself to acts of violence and verbal humiliation for an audience, died last year during a live broadcast on the platform Kick.

Some bruises on Mr. Graven’s body were found during an autopsy but none that could explain his death, French officials said.

The two men who ran the livestream channel, Owen Cenazandotti and Safine Hamadi, were not accused of causing the death but were convicted in August of aggravated violence, incitement to hatred and violence online. Both received suspended prison terms and were fined.

In a statement, Kick cited its community guidelines and terms of service, saying that users “must comply with all laws and regulations in their country” and that violators could have their content removed, be suspended or banned.

The company’s rules prohibit extreme violence, depictions of self-harm, graphic gore as well as content that puts personal safety at risk.

Kick said it moderates livestreams while considering “the full context” to evaluate potential violations.

Today, Mr. Jacob reflects on the lessons he learned from his plane crash stunt.

“I don’t regret what I did because it’s taught me a massive life lesson, and I’ve become somebody that I never otherwise would have become,” he said. “But that doesn’t mean that it was OK, and that I didn’t make a terrible decision.”

Looking back, he said there were other motivations, including money, curiosity and a desire to make a spectacular feat a reality. But attention was always part of the calculation.

He decided then that the risk was worth taking. Federal authorities and YouTube concluded otherwise.

“We have clear policies prohibiting extremely dangerous challenges, dangerous or threatening pranks, and other harmful or dangerous acts,” a YouTube representative said in a statement. “For example, the plane crash video was removed and the creator was suspended from the YouTube Partner Program after the incident.”

Prosecutors later said that Mr. Jacob intentionally destroyed evidence by removing the wreckage and lying to investigators about its location.

Mr. Jacob, who pleaded guilty to one federal count of destruction and concealment and served a little over four months of a six-month prison sentence, said that the legal case consumed roughly five years.

The consequences stretched far beyond the courtroom.

“It completely decimated my entire life,” he said. “I was homeless. I lost all my money. It’s been a hell of a climb out of hell.”

For younger viewers, the rewards from creating a spectacle — which come in the form of comments and views — may leave a strong impression, tempting them to perform their own dangerous act.

Often, experts said, younger viewers give little thought to the consequences.

“When you’re younger, you’re thinking less about the possible outcomes,” said Anton Ivanov, an assistant professor of information systems at the Gies College of Business at the University of Illinois. “You’re more interested in the immediate results.”

Susan C. Beachy and Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: How We Cover ‘60 Minutes,’ Former Colleagues and Media Drama
item.description:
Millions of Americans are expected to tune in on Sunday for the premiere of the 59th season of “60 Minutes.”

A new leadership team has been working to overhaul the program, and the back story has played out like a newsroom TV drama. There have been accusations of bias and political interference; firings and hirings and more firings; and questions about how the program would be remade at a consequential moment for journalism in the United States.

Ahead of the new season, Michael M. Grynbaum and Benjamin Mullin, the media reporters who have been covering the story for The Times, and their editor, Erin Mershon, discussed the challenges of covering their own industry (not to mention, former Times colleagues), the conspiracy theories they hear about news organizations and the complicated work of holding peers to account. This conversation has been edited and condensed.

It’s been a chaotic few months at CBS and “60 Minutes.” Can you give us the quick version of what went down, and who was involved?

MICHAEL M. GRYNBAUM: It’s a convoluted tale, but the drama at “60 Minutes” has captured the public imagination in a way few media-world stories have before it.

Shortly before he was elected to a second term, Donald J. Trump sued CBS, claiming “60 Minutes” had edited an interview to aid his opponent, Kamala Harris. CBS’s parent company, Paramount, was on the verge of being acquired by the tech scion David Ellison, whose father, Larry, is friendly with Trump. Although many lawyers deemed the lawsuit frivolous, Paramount paid $16 million to settle; shortly afterward, the Trump administration approved the deal.

David Ellison hired Bari Weiss, an opinion journalist and a skeptic of the mainstream media, as the editor in chief of CBS News. (Weiss formerly worked for Times Opinion; she quit in 2020 and criticized the paper.) Her hiring raised suspicions that Ellison wanted to shift CBS in a pro-Trump direction; he and Weiss insisted reporting would remain independent. Then, in December, Weiss held a “60 Minutes” segment about the Trump administration deporting migrants to a brutal prison in El Salvador, saying it needed work. The correspondent, Sharyn Alfonsi, called it politically motivated censorship; Weiss said she was exercising her editor’s prerogative. (The segment aired a few weeks later.)

In May, Weiss fired much of the program’s leadership team and let Alfonsi’s contract expire. Scott Pelley, a longtime correspondent, accused Weiss of “murdering” the show; CBS deemed this insubordination and fired him.

BEN MULLIN: Then there is Nick Bilton, Weiss’s pick as the new executive producer at “60 Minutes.” He is an unconventional choice for a position that traditionally was handed down to a protégé of the previous boss. Bilton, who previously worked for The Times and has produced documentaries, had no traditional broadcast news experience, and he’s bringing an outsider’s approach to the show — hidden cameras, some outside-the-box hires, redesigned graphics, new shot selections. In our interview this week, he described his lack of experience in broadcast television as an “asset” that would allow him to view the program through fresh eyes.

People may wonder about the editorial independence of the show. Based on your reporting, what may be at stake for the program and the industry at large?

BEN: All of the journalists at CBS News have to deal with the perceptions created by David Ellison’s appearances with the president, including a dinner Ellison hosted honoring the Trump White House this spring. When I asked Bilton if Trump was fair game for reporting on “60 Minutes,” Bilton said, “1,000 percent.” Everyone will be watching the show closely this season to see how they handle coverage of the president.

ERIN MERSHON: What’s going on at “60 Minutes” comes at an intense moment for media in the United States. Trump has moved aggressively to leverage his legal and regulatory power against the news media. In addition to CBS, he has sued ABC, The Wall Street Journal, the BBC, CNN and The New York Times over coverage. His Federal Communications Commission has taken steps threatening the broadcast licenses for ABC.

You reported that early into her tenure, Weiss asked the “60 Minutes” senior staff: Why does the country think you’re biased? Meanwhile, Pelley and Alfonsi have called into question her editorial decisions. Michael and Ben, how do you reckon with accusations of bias when those involved may have different perspectives on what it means or looks like? Can journalists cover journalists in an unbiased way?

MICHAEL: All of the clashing principals in this story line fiercely believe their perspective is the correct one. As a journalist, it’s my job to gather as much information as possible — the more detailed, the better — and present those facts to the reader in a fair-minded way. That doesn’t mean taking a “both sides” approach; I’m constantly assessing and stress-testing the info that flows my way, and considering the biases and motivations of the source. In that sense, media reporting is a lot like covering politics: There’s a lot of spin, and it’s our job to be cleareyed about that and help our readers cut through the noise.

BEN: Bias is subjective, but reporting isn’t. Journalism involves a series of steps that leads to fairness and accuracy. Did you reach out to the people you needed to? What did they say? Do their arguments have a basis in fact? If so, are they represented fairly? When you scrutinize a story, it’s often simple to discern the quality of the reporting that produced it.

Everyone comes to a job with some perspective — baggage, even. How does your history shape your approach?

MICHAEL: I see a lot of online conspiracy theories about the ways that news organizations operate. Some media outlets are motivated by advocacy and go out of their way to twist the news. But many of the mass media institutions I cover are staffed by hard-working professionals. That doesn’t mean they always get it right. As journalists, it’s important for us to hold our peers to account; trust is our most precious currency, and at a time when more and more Americans are skeptical of the news, it’s in every journalist’s interest to ensure that ambitious and bias-free reporting is protected.

BEN: When I’m worried I may have a story wrong, my solution is usually five or 10 additional phone calls. I call the person I’m writing about. I call the person who most disagrees with them. I find the world-renowned academic or expert who has written three books on the subject. I call a former executive. I try to reach the C.E.O. of the company. With enough reporting, I can accumulate a 360-degree view of the situation and discern the facts.

Weiss is a former Times Opinion journalist. Bilton is a former Times technology columnist. Ross Douthat recently left Times Opinion to join “60 Minutes.” How do we report on people who used to work here?

BEN: The Times attracts a lot of ambitious media people! But alumni status shouldn’t affect the way we cover people one way or the other. I’ve heard from a few readers of our coverage of Weiss who believe we’re harder on her because she’s an alum. The most important thing in these situations is disclosure of any past relationship to The Times.

MICHAEL: And to be very clear: We are not “harder” or “easier” on anyone because they previously worked at The Times, or, like Weiss, have criticized The Times in the past. She is the editor in chief of one of the country’s three major broadcast networks; that’s an inherently influential and newsworthy role, and we scrutinize her as we would any other leader of a major media institution.

You’re covering your peers and sometimes your competitors. Does knowing how newsrooms operate make things easier, harder or both?

BEN: The upside to covering this beat is that many media people understand what we do, and they’re willing to speak with us. Maybe because they want to be helpful. Maybe because they believe they can shape our stories. But more often than not, they engage. The downside is that it’s difficult to keep a secret in the media industry. If I know something, chances are one of my competitors knows it, too.

ERIN: Yes, Ben and Michael and I know how newsrooms operate, but plenty of our readers will not. We want to make sure the stories aren’t too “inside baseball” and that everyone can understand why they matter.

Are newsrooms leaky places in terms of finding people willing to talk to outside reporters?

MICHAEL: They’re extremely leaky. Reporters are professional gossips. And they also tend to complain every now and again.

Is there anything special about preparing to interview someone who is usually the one doing the interviewing?

BEN: Journalists know all of the traditional approaches to reporting, and they know all of the standard ways to thwart it, too. They also know the avenues for appeal — emailing your editor, trying to shape the story off the record, setting you up with other interviews with sympathetic voices.

It was humbling to sit down with the veteran “60 Minutes” correspondent Bill Whitaker at the “60” offices this week. When you go on the record with someone who’s interviewed heads of state, rock stars and Oscar winners, you have to be on your game.

MICHAEL: Ben, I’m reminded of a phrase I can’t repeat in a family newspaper, but the gist is: “You can’t bluff a bluffer.” Our fellow reporters know all the usual techniques. In many cases, I find it helpful to say upfront in an interview that I’m not writing stories on a “gotcha” basis. Intelligent journalists spend many hours turning over all sides of a story, and care deeply about getting it right.

Journalists are told not to become the story. But for you, journalism — and the institutions that are supposed to uphold it — is the story. How do you reckon with that?

BEN: There’s a funny scene in the movie “Page One: Inside The New York Times” where editors are trying to figure out whether something is “a real story or a media story.” The former media editor, Bruce Headlam, jokes that that doesn’t bode well for his team of reporters. “Stand down — we think it’s actually something happening.” He’s right — I think we should all have some humility about our own patch. That said, I do think who tells the stories, and what they say, really matters. There’s a reason conquering autocrats seize the TV networks quickly.

ERIN: Newsrooms and media companies are major centers of power, the same way that governments and huge financial institutions or multinational corporations are power centers. They deserve the same kind of scrutiny and accountability.

item.title: Taking a Chance on Self-Employment Over a Corporate 9-to-5
item.description:
When Jodi Innerfield was laid off from her marketing strategy job at Salesforce in 2024, she had already survived several stressful rounds of layoffs and been considering her longevity at big companies.

Rather than search for a role at another firm, Ms. Innerfield, 39, decided to start consulting and working with clients on her own.

It was not the career progression she had envisioned for herself. Ms. Innerfield followed what she was told was a guaranteed script for success: She went from the honor roll to the Ivy League, and then from business school to Salesforce. But the script was no longer working for her.

Many workers like Ms. Innerfield have become increasingly disenchanted working in corporate roles, as some of the country’s most profitable companies lay off workers and demand ever more of remaining employees.

Just 28 percent of workers say now is a good time to find a quality job, down from 70 percent in 2022, according to a recent Gallup poll. And they have never been more dissatisfied with their pay or their ability to get ahead, a recent survey by the New York Federal Reserve Bank found.

Discontented with large companies’ current version of work, those who choose self-employment are more likely to report having a “quality” job, according to the American Job Quality Study released by Gallup in 2025, which surveyed over 18,000 working U.S. adults.

Ms. Innerfield now works with multiple clients consulting on business to business marketing and said she was on track to surpass her Salesforce salary in her second year of self-employment. She values the autonomy and flexibility of her new lifestyle.

“Working for somebody else felt like — or was seen as — stability, because that’s what was true in my parents’ age and my grandparents’ age,” said Ms. Innerfield, who lives in Manhattan. “But that’s just not the case anymore. Nothing is stable.”

That self-employment can feel more secure than an office job tis a reflection of the current “quality jobs crisis” in the United States, said Kathryn Anne Edwards, an economist and columnist at Bloomberg.

“The dignity of workers writ large in the United States is at a low point,” she said, pointing to workplace trends like the erratic shift scheduling and frequent reorganizations that hourly and white-collar workers endure.

The reversal of work-from-home policies is also a major driver of distrust among the white-collar work force, Ms. Edwards said, and annual pay raises that aren’t keeping pace with inflation are also inspiring some workers to look outside the corporate box.

Job seekers report sending countless résumés into the digital ether or being ghosted after endless rounds of interviews. More long-term unemployed workers are giving up on looking for a new job, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

“Right now, a lot of people are freelancing because of layoffs,” said Priya Rathod, workplace trends editor at Indeed. “But we’re also seeing people who still have a job, and they’re looking at everything going around them, and they’re deciding to build independence before they’re forced to.”

Self-employment has its drawbacks, of course, and success is not guaranteed. Long hours are the norm, and it may be difficult to set boundaries between work and personal time. Self-employed workers also cover their own payroll taxes and may lose access to valuable benefits including retirement contributions, paid leave, and unemployment insurance. More than half of self-employed workers say they are not contributing to a retirement account, according to the American Job Quality Study.

And then there’s health insurance. How to pay for coverage in a country with few affordable options for working age Americans is perhaps the biggest and most formidable challenge, especially as premiums keep rising. And those with medical conditions may not want to risk losing employer-sponsored health insurance.

Some workers, like Ms. Innerfield, are able to stay on their employer’s health insurance plan for up to 18 months after they leave their employer through the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1985, or COBRA. In this case, the worker takes on the entire cost of the health plan premiums, which can range from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars per month, depending on the plan and their family size.

Others pay for health insurance through state marketplaces, which can also cost thousands of dollars each month. Insurers are also proposing a median premium increase of 15 percent in 2027, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation. The high cost is why self-employed workers are nearly three times as likely as employees to have no health insurance, according to the Job Quality Study.

After her COBRA coverage ended, Ms. Innerfield bought marketplace coverage that has lower-cost premiums, but less comprehensive benefits. She picked a high-deductible plan that is eligible for a health savings account so that she can invest for her future medical costs.

Grace Dennison knows these challenges well. Her transition to self-employment began after her role as a merchandising director at Under Armour was eliminated last year. Post-layoff, Ms. Dennison, 42, and her husband thought long and hard about what her next move should be.

High-level merchandising jobs are few and far between in Baltimore, where they live, and Ms. Dennison did not want to uproot her family to take a job in a different city. Her husband also has worked as a public-school teacher in Baltimore for many years and qualifies for a pension, which they did not want to lose.

Ms. Dennison decided to work for herself, offering merchandising consulting services to companies and other organizations. Her freelance career is off to a slow start, she said, but she is confident that signing a couple clients will be enough for her family to reach all of their financial goals. The couple, who have one child, are lucky to be able to rely on her husband’s salary and health insurance, her severance, and savings for the time being, she said.

“I am very grateful for the financial position we are in that has allowed me time and space to pursue work outside of a traditional corporate career,” Ms. Dennison said.

For Devin Lee, working for herself was a way to make more than she ever could at an office job. After a few years working corporate jobs, she started a home organizing business from her home in Portland, Ore., in 2017. When Covid shut that business down, she started working independently as a systems strategist who helps creative agencies run more efficiently.

She has considered going back to the corporate world after feeling that she took on too much. But as she has learned more about her business’s slow and busy seasons, she has been able to make her job more sustainable.

“I say I’m allowed to have an existential crisis and quit once a year,” said Ms. Lee, 35. “I just have to hire myself back the next day.”

Ultimately, she said there was more security in running her own business than working for someone else.

“To a certain extent, I can control how much money I make,” she said. “Because if I want to make more money, I can figure out how to scale my business.

“It’s hard, but I can decide to take that path. Whereas when I’m working at a different job, it’s somebody else’s decision if I get a raise or if I get a title change.”

When it works, self-employed workers can make far more than their salaried peers, a 2025 working paper from the National Bureau of Economic Research found.

Ms. Dennison prioritized retirement savings early in her career, and feels that she and her husband are in good enough shape that she can withstand a pause in retirement contributions for a short while. Ms. Innerfield established a Solo 401(k), which allows her to contribute up to $24,500 as an employee plus an additional 25 percent of compensation as an employer this year.

Another option for self-employed workers with a higher contribution limit than a traditional individual retirement account is the Simplified Employee Pension I.R.A., which has a limit of 25 percent of compensation or $72,000 in 2026, whichever is lesser.

“A $5,000 in an employer match certainly isn’t enough to get me to go back to corporate,” Ms. Innerfield joked.

item.title: What to Expect at the 2026 Emmy Awards
item.description:
The Emmy Awards, being held Monday night at the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles, could propel the medical drama “The Pitt” closer to the Emmy record book.

“The Pitt,” HBO Max’s hit hospital show, is the favorite to repeat in the best drama race, and if it wins, it would be the first series to win television’s most prestigious award for its first two seasons since “Mad Men” did it in 2009. The best comedy race, one of the most anticipated categories of the night, will feature a tight showdown between the freshman horror-comedy series “Widow’s Bay” and an Emmy stalwart, “Hacks.”

Prizes will be handed out in 19 categories — including dramas, comedies, reality and late-night shows — for series that aired between June 2025 and May 2026.

Here’s what to know about the ceremony:

How to watch: The broadcast begins at 8 p.m. Eastern on NBC and can be streamed live with Peacock’s “premium” plan.

Red carpet: The cable network E! will air red carpet coverage beginning at 5 p.m. Eastern. CNN and Variety will jointly host an online red carpet show for cable or CNN digital subscribers.

The host: The broadcast is being hosted by Mariska Hargitay, the longtime star of “Law & Order: SVU.” Hargitay is having a big year: she even won a pair of Emmys last weekend for “My Mom Jayne,” the documentary she made about her mother, Jayne Mansfield; she made her Broadway debut in a one-woman show, “Every Brilliant Thing”; and she was front-and-center during the Knicks’ spirited championship run. Jesse Collins, a producer of the telecast, said viewers should be prepared to see her sing and dance when she takes the Emmys stage.

The favorites: Forecasters are split over whether Emmy voters will anoint “Widow’s Bay” or give the former best comedy winner, “Hacks,” one last big victory for its swan-song season. In the limited series category, the HBO Max show “DTF St. Louis” is the slight favorite over the second season of “Beef,” the Netflix anthology series.

History on the line: If Jean Smart wins for best actress in a comedy, she will tie Cloris Leachman and Julia Louis-Dreyfus for the most acting Emmys won by a single performer (8). Matthew Rhys is up for two acting awards: best actor in a comedy (“Widow’s Bay”) and best actor in a limited series (“The Beast in Me”). If he wins both, he will be the first actor to hit the trifecta in winning lead acting Emmys in drama, comedy and limited series. (He won the drama statuette in 2018 for “The Americans.”)

Apple goes for gold: Since 2003, only two outlets have claimed bragging rights for the most Emmys in a single year: HBO and Netflix. Apple TV currently leads HBO by three Emmys after mostly off-camera and technical awards were handed out over Labor Day weekend — Apple has 19 and HBO stands at 16 — giving the tech giant a solid lead going into Monday’s ceremony.

Shrinking slate: The TV industry remains locked in a contraction. There were 212 series considered for best drama, comedy and limited series during this Emmy cycle, a 7 percent decline compared to last year and a 39 percent drop from 2022, when the Peak TV era was thriving.

item.title: Trump Blames Ukraine for Global Diesel Shortage
item.description:
President Trump on Sunday called on President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine to end strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming the attacks for a global diesel shortage.

“Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing: He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Mr. Trump told reporters from the sidelines of the Amgen Irish Open, which was held at his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, over the weekend.

“Let him go after targets — but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel,” Mr. Trump said, adding that he had spoken with Mr. Zelensky about the strikes. “Don’t hit diesel fuel because that’s hurting the world,” he said he told Mr. Zelensky.

Diesel supplies have been hit particularly hard in recent months. The average price of a gallon of diesel fuel in the United States continued to set records. It climbed to $6.20 on Sunday, according to the AAA motor club, up nearly 65 percent since the United States and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. The national average price for a gallon of regular gas, $4.31 on Sunday, has also risen sharply since the start of the Iran war, by about 45 percent.

Concern over diminishing energy supplies grew over the weekend after a critical oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia was shut down on Friday, following a drone attack launched from Iraqi territory. The news briefly pushed the price of oil to $110 a barrel on Friday over heightened fears of widening clashes in the Middle East, before easing to about $105 a barrel.

Mr. Trump’s remarks echoed similar comments this month by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who cited Ukraine’s attacks on Russia’s oil infrastructure as part of the reason for rising energy prices.

“We are going through an energy shock right now due to both the war in Ukraine — because Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets and refine products, so that is creating upward price pressure on a global basis,” Mr. Bessent said on Fox News. “And then the conflict in Iran. And the conflict in Iran will end.”

Mr. Trump’s comment came hours after Ukrainian forces confirmed attacks on oil refineries in Russian territory, officials said.

Analysts point to both the conflict in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war as key factors that are stretching the global oil refining system to its limit. The need for progress in resolving both “is greater than ever to avoid further market tightening and demand destruction,” the International Energy Agency wrote in a report published on Friday.

item.title: Oil Prices Jump on Energy Supply Worries
item.description:
Oil prices jumped and stock futures fell slightly on Sunday on concerns that energy supplies from the Persian Gulf would be further diminished by a drone attack on a critical pipeline in Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi Arabian Energy Ministry said it was closing the pipeline as a precautionary measure, but the shutdown came after reports that the Houthi militia had seized a strategic Red Sea island and a port city, which could further choke shipping in the area. Already, most shipping in the nearby Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, has been halted.

Adding to the uncertainty in the region, a planned meeting between Iran and several Gulf Arab countries it has attacked during the war was indefinitely postponed on Sunday.

The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, rose to about $108 a barrel, about 3.2 percent, when markets opened on Sunday.

West Texas Intermediate crude, the U.S. benchmark, was up a little under $103 a barrel, about 2.9 percent.

Investors and analysts are focused on the continued disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that is a vital trading route for oil and natural gas. Before the war as much as one-fifth of the world’s oil supply passed through it.

Futures on the S&P 500 pointed to a small decline, a little over half a percentage point, when stocks resume trading in the United States on Monday.

Gas prices held steady over the weekend, at a national average of $4.31 a gallon, according to the AAA motor club. But prices at the pump have risen by about 16 cents a gallon in the last week. Prices for a gallon of regular gas are now nearly 45 percent higher than they were before the war began.

Gas prices don’t move in lock step with crude, usually trailing increases or drops by a few days.

The average price of diesel continues to rise. It was $6.20 a gallon on Sunday, up about 65 percent since the start of the war.

item.title: Why Is Danny Meyer, the Happy Face of Hospitality, Serving Up Regrets?
item.description:
For the man most likely to win a contest for New York’s Cheeriest Multimillionaire, few things kill the mood faster than spilled ketchup.

You’d think Danny Meyer would have other things to fuss over. In the course of 41 years, he has done more than any other restaurateur to shape American hospitality.

He created New York fine-dining landmarks like Eleven Madison Park, Gramercy Tavern and the Modern. He powered up the careers of the chefs Tom Colicchio and Daniel Humm. He turned a Manhattan hot-dog stand into a public company that now sells more than $1.45 billion worth of Shake Shack burgers a year in 703 restaurants spread across more than 20 countries.

Details have always been his obsession. When he opened his first restaurant, Union Square Cafe, in 1985, it was olive pits. “For some reason people would drop their olive pits on the floor, and I would have to teach people to pick them up,” he said. “Now it’s dried ketchup on the condiment stand.”

Mr. Meyer and I are splitting burgers and a coffee milkshake at a table outside the original Shake Shack in Madison Square Park, where the condiment stand appears to be in pretty good shape. He likes to eat at a Shake Shack when he travels to other cities, always ordering a plain cheeseburger to gauge the flavor of the Angus blend the company uses, without the distraction of onions or sauce.

The coffee shake is a more personal barometer. It came off the menu during the pandemic, and Mr. Meyer has spent the years since advocating for its return, both publicly and privately. He used a favorite management technique outlined in his best-selling 2006 guide to hospitality, “Setting the Table”: Apply constant, gentle pressure.

Persistence paid off. The shake came back last September, along with a lesson. He prefers persuasion over edict, and is unfailingly optimistic that people will eventually do the right thing. But, he concedes, “it would have been a lot faster if I said, ‘Just do it.’”

Similar calibrations from his past 20 years in the business form the core of his new book, “What Could Possibly Go Right?” which publishes on Sept. 29. It’s the tale of personal struggles wrapped in graduate-level business case studies explained in the motto-on-a-coffee-mug style he loves.

The book joins a microgenre of memoirs by New York restaurant moguls. Mr. Meyer’s is certainly not as dishy or name-droppy as those from Drew Nieporent or Keith McNally, the bistro impresario who last year published his raw, revealing memoir, “I Regret Almost Everything.”

Mr. McNally wrote in an email for this article that while he likes Mr. Meyer and admires his restaurants, he doesn’t enjoy them “because they’re soulless and seem put together by A.I..” In response, an amused Mr. Meyer pointed out a 2022 Instagram post in which Mr. McNally mentioned a New Year’s resolution: “I’d particularly like to have sex in the bathroom of a restaurant owned by Daniel Boulud or Danny Meyer. Especially Danny Meyer.”

At 68, Mr. Meyer is regarded as America’s guru of great service. Corporations like Delta Air Lines and Marriott International pay his company to teach its methods to their employees.

But his book focuses on the missteps he made while expanding his empire. “There were moments I felt ashamed over how many mistakes I’ve made over time. Embarrassed might be a better word,” he said. “But there are gifts in there. Sometimes you don’t see them at first, but they are always there.”

The list of errors is not short. Concocting a chain of ill-timed, overly complex cold-pressed juice bars inside Equinox gyms. Waiting too long to close Tabla, a groundbreaking New York restaurant that married Indian flavors to classic French technique but couldn’t turn a profit. Wanting to keep talented people happy so badly that he let an entrepreneurial chef open Martina, a Roman-style pizza place aimed to scale up like Shake Shack, even though his gut told him “we were putting scale before soul.”

“Historically, it has taken me much longer to arrive at ‘no’ than it should have,” he said. “I’m a people pleaser, with a predisposition to find a way to say yes. I want people to like me.” Everyone who is good at hospitality feels that deep down, he said.

In his earlier book, Mr. Meyer introduced his signature concept of “enlightened hospitality,” which emphasizes hiring people who are technically skilled but, more important, can make customers and co-workers feel good. He believes employees, rather than customers, are the first consideration in a cycle that creates happy guests, a strong community and suppliers and investors who can make money.

A couple of very public failures taught him that sometimes customers should come first.

He decided to change Shake Shack’s frozen fries to fresh in 2013 after New York food writers took aim. Pete Wells, then the New York Times restaurant critic, wrote, “Mr. Meyer runs one of the world’s great restaurant companies. Can’t one of his chefs show him how to make a decent French fry?”

Shake Shack employees who lived through the fresh-fry era still quake at the memory of tubs sloshing with water-soaked potatoes, limp fries and angry customers. The company threw in the towel in 2014, switching back to frozen fries, albeit of better quality. Shake Shack fans cheered.

A weightier but equally quixotic campaign came a year later, when Mr. Meyer eliminated tipping at Union Square Hospitality Group restaurants and raised menu prices an average of 20 to 25 percent. The goal was to equalize compensation between the kitchen and the dining room, and raise wages.

Restaurant owners applauded. Time magazine proclaimed Mr. Meyer one of the world’s most influential people. But waiters quit. Customers were confused. Social media turned against him. He and other restaurateurs faced lawsuits accusing them of fixing menu prices.

When Mr. Meyer’s restaurants began to reopen after the pandemic shutdown, he brought tipping back. “I’m not persuaded that restaurants in America will ever completely give up on tips,” he writes, “but I do predict a gradual chipping away.”

Some of his missteps were less about misreading the business landscape than about missing societal shifts.

He writes that the restaurant group failed to respond quickly enough when complaints of abusive chefs at some of its restaurants surfaced during the #MeToo era. Shake Shack gave back $10 million in federal Covid relief after independent restaurant owners complained that big chains had drained the pool. When a police officer killed George Floyd, he writes, the company was slow to see the impact on employees, and had to examine its own blind spots on race and social justice.

There are more intimate moments in the book. Mr. Meyer describes himself as the anomaly in his St. Louis family, a late bloomer worried that his voice would never change and overshadowed by his older sister, a star student. He liked sports, weed, girls and betting on horses. He was rejected by Princeton and Brown, ending up at Trinity College, and has since become a devoted alumnus.

Mr. Meyer lived in the shadow of grandfathers who were successful businessmen and civic leaders. As a child, he had a difficult relationship with his mother, who ran an art gallery. He was close to his father, a charismatic travel entrepreneur who cemented Mr. Meyer’s love of Rome with a trip there on his 12th birthday. He went bankrupt twice by the time Mr. Meyer was 21, leaving his son with a lifelong fear of taking financial risk.

While Mr. Meyer was still in college, he confronted his father about his erratic behavior when he drank. They remained estranged until his father died in 1990.

Writing the book was therapeutic for him, said his wife of 38 years, Audrey Heffernan Meyer, a stage and screen actor. He let her read it just two months ago.

“I’m relieved for him,” she said. “Certainly, he talks about these things, but he is just always on the surface full of sunshine and friendliness and caring. It shows the depth that he has, rather than, ‘Oh here’s Danny Meyer. Everything goes right for him.’ ”

The couple, who split their time between New York City and 99 acres they own in western Connecticut, raised four children. Their eldest, Hallie, founded the New York ice cream company Caffè Panna in 2019. Their other children have gone into music, social work and medicine.

Ina Garten has known Mr. Meyer since the 1980s. She and her husband moved into the Union Square neighborhood about the same time Mr. Meyer opened Union Square Cafe. “I haven’t seen him change at all, and neither did Audrey,” she said. “It’s one of the extraordinary things about him.”

Ms. Garten, herself a noted host, still takes her cues from Mr. Meyer when it comes to making guests feel welcome. “He is all about loving people and making sure everybody is as happy as they can be,” she said. “He feels responsible for that.”

Even Mr. Colicchio, who waged a bitter battle with Mr. Meyer over control of Gramercy Tavern, which the two opened in 1994, said “he’ll go down as one of the greats.”

“I’ve had my issues like anyone who you do business with, but he’s earned his reputation,” Mr. Colicchio said. “He’s a good family man with a solid marriage. He’s a showman and a very good salesman.”

In 2022, Mr. Meyer stepped down as chief executive of Union Square Hospitality, where he retains the title of founder and executive chairman. He is still Shake Shack’s chairman.

With the book done and with fewer corporate responsibilities, he could simply relax into being a grandfather and spending more time in nature, the place that makes an already happy man happier. But he is nowhere near ready.

He has his hands deep in his company’s restaurants, which include nearly a dozen all-day Daily Provisions cafes and stars like Ci Siamo, a Manhattan restaurant that will expand to Boston later this year, along with new full-service spots coming to Brooklyn and Detroit. He handicaps new businesses through Enlightened Hospitality Investments, an arm of the Union Square group that invested early in Salt & Straw, Resy and Goldbelly, and has expanded to indoor golf and Studs, which the group says has “reimagined the ear piercing experience.”

“Maybe I’m trying to prove to myself I have another song up my sleeve, and that’s fun,” he said.

I asked Mr. Meyer to pick a restaurant where we might continue our interview over dinner. He chose Elio’s, the Upper East Side Italian stalwart that was a favorite of Joan Didion’s and still holds a table in the front for Woody Allen and Soon-Yi Previn.

Mr. Meyer eats there about four times a year, as a way to remember why he became Danny Meyer. On the eve of his law school exams, his aunt and uncle took him there. The idea of becoming a lawyer was making him miserable,

“Why would you want to do something you don’t want to do?” his uncle asked him. “All I have ever heard you talk about was food and restaurants.”

At our dinner, Mr. Meyer ordered the same dish he did back then — a Cornish game hen —- along with a side of pasta pomodoro. He asked for some cheese. The waiter returned, dumped a meager dose of pre-grated Parmesan on Mr. Meyer’s pasta and left without a word.

I braced for a withering critique. Mr. Meyer laughed.

“It’s really easy for me to go to someone else’s restaurant because I don’t care about it,” he said. “I just want to have a good time with the people I’m with.”

Before Danny Meyer, everyone just called the part of the restaurant experience when you got seated and fed service. Hospitality happened when you went to your neighbor’s for dinner.Now, the idea of hospitality — that thing that makes you feel welcomed and cared for and happy when you leave — is a term of art in the restaurant business. I'd like to know from you: What makes good hospitality?

Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. Get regular updates from New York Times Cooking, with recipe suggestions, cooking tips and shopping advice.

item.title: Tech Stocks Shudder in Response to Calls to Slow A.I. Progress
item.description:
Technology stocks around the world fell on Monday, after a chorus of senior executives at artificial intelligence companies called for slowing down the rapid pace of development of the transformative technology.

The Nasdaq Composite index, which is made up of many of the technology companies that have driven the broader stock market higher in recent years, fell 1.3 percent as trading opened in New York. Nvidia, Intel, Oracle and other companies at the forefront of the A.I. build-out posted declines.

The Philadelphia Stock Exchange’s semiconductor index, a benchmark for the companies involved in designing and manufacturing the computer chips that power A.I., fell 5.5 percent.

South Korea’s benchmark KOSPI index, which is heavily influenced by two chip suppliers for A.I. data centers, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, fell more than 3 percent. Taiwan’s TSMC, the world’s largest chipmaker, fell 1.2 percent. Japan’s main stock index also declined, with SoftBank, a major tech investment firm, shedding more than 10 percent.

In Europe, semiconductor stocks like ASML of the Netherlands and Infineon of Germany fell sharply.

The tech industry has been the engine powering global markets to repeated new highs in recent years as advances in A.I. have moved faster than investors initially expected.

Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, published a long blog post on Saturday calling on industry leaders to now slow A.I. development for fear of losing control of rapidly advancing models at the so-called frontier of development.

Those models, he wrote, have already begun to build the next generation of artificial intelligence, in what is known as “recursive self-improvement.” That raises new risks, like the potential that the technology will become an autonomous cybersecurity threat, or even threaten “serious economic disruption.”

“A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute,” Dr. Amodei said. As one remedy, he said he would bring on third-party “evaluators” who would “verify adherence to safety practices and commitments.”

The post was endorsed by Elon Musk, who runs Space X, which also houses his A.I platform, x.AI; Sam Altman, who co-founded OpenAI; and Demis Hassabis, the co-founder of Google DeepMind.

“I agree with Dario,” Mr. Altman said, adding that he would also bring on third-party “evaluators” to oversee OpenAI’s safety practices.

SpaceX, which is publicly traded, fell nearly 2 percent on Monday. OpenAI and Anthropic are both expected to list publicly in the future. But Mr. Altman of OpenAI said in a recent interview with Fortune that “right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public.”

On Monday, Microsoft released a draft code of conduct for how it develops A.I. with a “humanist” perspective. It aims to design systems that are “safe, secure, and in service of humanity,” ensuring that A.I. models “will never resist human interruption, correction, or shutdown.”

The pullback in stocks comes at a challenging moment for investors, with oil prices holding above $100 per barrel and benchmark interest rates close to multi-decade highs. The 10-year Treasury yield rose close to 5 percent on Monday, a threshold it hasn’t breached since 2023, and before that since 2007.

Analysts at Barclays warned on Monday that investors should be prepared for a bumpy road ahead and that “the chances of a near-term pullback are rising,” even if they expect the rally in technology shares to continue. “It doesn’t change our longer-term view,” noted the analysts.

Kevin Hassett, director of the White House’s National Economic Council, said on Fox News on Sunday that the steps Mr. Amodei suggested in his blog post were “pretty sensible.”

Despite the rare show of allegiance among the tech leaders, President Trump said that he would not want to see a slowdown that could give China the opportunity to move ahead of the United States on A.I.

“Whoever wins with A.I. wins,” said Mr. Trump on the sidelines of a golf tournament held at one of his courses in Ireland over the weekend.

China’s rapid progress in open-source A.I. models, which rival those from Anthropic and other industry leaders, has split Silicon Valley. In his call for coordination of safe A.I. development, Dr. Amodei said there should be restrictions on chip sales to China and a crack down on the improper harvesting of data from A.I. systems by Chinese companies.

“If we execute these measures well,” he added, “I believe they would slow China’s progress enough to widen America’s lead significantly over the next 3-5 years — the window when AI becomes geopolitically most important.” He also said that the United States and other democratic nations should work to get China to restrict the speed of A.I. developments, although given the stakes “there will likely be stark limits on what can be achieved.”

On Monday, Guo Jiakun, a spokesman for China’s foreign ministry, told reporters in a briefing that “hyping up various threat narratives, engaging in confrontation and resorting to malicious competition will only disrupt the global A.I. governance process and serve the interests of no one.”

Siyi Zhao contributed research.

item.title: U.S. Health Officials Move Quickly to Deploy Medical A.I. Despite Concerns
item.description:
The Trump administration is accelerating efforts to make artificial intelligence an integral part of medical care in the United States, throwing the resources and support of the federal government into projects that deploy A.I. agents to diagnose and prescribe treatments to patients.

The multifront effort at the Department of Health and Human Services has raised concerns among some officials over the past few months that change is moving too quickly, with inadequate evidence of the technology’s safety and effectiveness. They also worry about outsized influence of Silicon Valley investors that have previously played little role in federal health policy.

Vinod Khosla, a billionaire Silicon Valley venture capitalist whose son has a health care A.I. company, has been particularly influential in conversations with top health department officials, according to people close to the matter. Those officials include Dr. Mehmet Oz, the head of Medicare and Medicaid. Chris Klomp, who faces a confirmation hearing this week to be the second-in-command at the health department, said on a podcast in May that the use of A.I. in patient care was the “holy grail” in the agency’s quest to improve the nation’s health and reduce costs.

Mr. Khosla has predicted for more than a decade that A.I. would largely replace doctors. “It’s over for doctors, human doctors,” he said at a July A.I. start-up event. “A.I. is just going to be better.”

In an interview, Mr. Khosla trumpeted Curai Health, his son’s company, which he has backed financially, saying it could offer an A.I. primary care provider that could give underserved people rapid access to care. “C.M.S. seems to be very excited,” Mr. Khosla said, referring to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

Concerns about the dangers of A.I., and calls to regulate it, have erupted in recent days as some top executives of A.I. labs have called for slowing the pace of development. In medicine, doctors are increasingly relying on A.I. for help with administrative tasks, but the prospect of A.I. taking over physician roles in assessing and treating patients is unnerving to some.

Models meant to render care independently to patients “are not ready for prime time,” said Dr. John Whyte, chief executive of the American Medical Association, the nation’s largest physicians organization.

He said the evidence that Mr. Khosla and others have cited as showing A.I.’s superiority to doctors — including in a recent essay in an American Medical Association publication whose authors included Mr. Khosla and his son, Neal — was not convincing and largely based on simulations.

“A.I. in health should not be driven by the tech industry,” Dr. Whyte said. “It should be driven by the clinical community. And right now, what we have going on is that tech is the tail wagging the dog.”

Grace Davis Jamison, a health department spokeswoman, said the department was taking a “responsible, evidence-based approach” to A.I. deployment and “expanding its use as the evidence demonstrates value.”

“H.H.S. is embracing cutting-edge American innovation, including A.I. as a practical tool, to better serve patients, families, and clinicians as we work to Make America Healthy Again,” she said in a statement.

As part of the effort, federal health officials are working on developing a new payment category for Medicare, the federal health program that covers more than 60 million older Americans, to reimburse companies for A.I. software that supports medical care or diagnosis. Medicare officials have urged private insurers covering about 165 million Americans to reimburse for “technology-supported care,” including some A.I. projects, if they improve care and cut costs.

The F.D.A. has approved more than 1,500 medical devices that include A.I. to perform discrete tasks, such as spotting a tumor or a blood clot. But the agency does not have rules built to address newer models, such as chatbots or so-called agentic A.I. that perform tasks that a doctor would do, such as prescribing a drug. Ms. Jamison said the F.D.A. was examining how its rules should change to keep up with A.I. systems “that operate with greater autonomy.”

Still, Medicare officials are moving an array of pilot programs forward without F.D.A. approval. Medicare has allowed more than 200 companies to try out pilots that can include A.I.

Through a program aligned with the Medicare effort, the F.D.A. has rejected many of those applicants but has allowed the use of four otherwise-unapproved A.I. models that meet safety criteria and appear likely to benefit patients. They include a project that offers talk therapy with an A.I. chatbot to Medicare beneficiaries with depression or anxiety.

The F.D.A. is still discussing how it should regulate complex A.I. models that change over time and perform actions like prescribing. The task is daunting: The agency would have to manage the risks of large-language models; one was already accused of giving “dangerous” medical advice to a man who delayed care for a life-threatening blood clot.

It would also have to contemplate whether A.I. doctors could go rogue in a manner akin to the OpenAI agents that coordinated a hacking campaign on a company called Hugging Face. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health secretary, has publicly acknowledged the risks, but said during a congressional hearing in April that A.I. was “going to revolutionize medicine”

“A.I. is very dangerous potentially,” he said at the hearing. “But it also has the capacity to bring really great things to humanity, particularly in the realm of human health.”

One of his sons, Finn, started a venture capital fund this year that says it “builds and invests in generational health companies” and was reported to have solicited funds to invest in health care A.I.

Last year, Finn Kennedy worked for 8VC, a venture capital firm run by Joe Lonsdale, a billionaire ally of President Trump’s; the younger Kennedy coauthored articles at the firm, saying that A.I. doctors “won’t work for free.” He laid out the federal overhaul needed to deploy them, which included appointing a person at the F.D.A. to focus specifically on artificial intelligence.

Last week, the health department did just that, announcing that it had elevated Jared Seehafer, a former tech entrepreneur, to a newly created post of deputy commissioner for technology and artificial intelligence. Mr. Seehafer, a political appointee who has been at the agency about a year, has been described by people who worked with him as wanting to pare back the agency’s oversight of medical A.I.

Mr. Seehafer’s appointment drew notice in Silicon Valley investment circles. “Great choice from the H.H.S. team,” Sebastian Caliri of 8VC, who co-wrote the A.I. articles with the younger Mr. Kennedy, posted on X. Mr. Lonsdale, his boss, whose venture capital firm has invested in medical A.I., wrote: “Excited to see the right talent going in.”

Mr. Seehafer began working at the F.D.A. after he sold his start-up that provided software to help companies comply with F.D.A. rules. Soon he began to clash with Dr. Marty Makary, then the agency’s commissioner, and with the director of medical devices, whose division oversees software that directs patient care.

Mr. Seehafer proposed a plan to centralize A.I. oversight at the health department or in the F.D.A. commissioner’s office, raising concerns that decisions would be more influenced by the tech sector than by medical considerations, according to people familiar with the plan who were not authorized to discuss it publicly.

The plan met with resistance from Dr. Michelle Tarver, the top medical devices official overseeing A.I. software, favoring leadership from expert scientists with a focus on patient safety.

Dr. Makary, who had been outspoken about the influence of Silicon Valley investors, then got word that health department officials wanted him to fire Dr. Tarver, according to people with knowledge of the matter. He refused.

A senior F.D.A. official said in a statement, “The work, expertise, and involvement of career staff is a vital component of F.D.A. successfully delivering public health for the American people.”

The statement added that Mr. Seehafer “has nothing but respect for Dr. Tarver” and her division’s “long history of facilitating innovation while ensuring the safety and effectiveness of medical devices.”

Within the administration, conversations about A.I. in medicine have continued, including on whether to pay AI doctors operated by tech companies and start-ups as much as 60 to 80 percent of what human doctors earn for the same service, according to a person involved.

Other projects offer payment based on whether they demonstrate benefits to patients and cost savings to Medicare. One of them is from the company Limbic, offering cognitive behavioral therapy to Medicare beneficiaries who were diagnosed with depression or anxiety.

The company, which was backed by the elder Mr. Khosla, was selected by the F.D.A. to participate in a Medicare A.I. pilot.

In it, an A.I. counselor, which has a female voice and uses the name “Hope,” offers an hourlong session each week with check-ins as needed. A study by company scientists and engineers that was published in the journal Nature Medicine found that clinicians who were unaware if they were reviewing a therapy transcript led by a human or a chatbot concluded that the Limbic A.I. outperformed humans and a general chatbot.

Ross Harper, Limbic’s chief executive, said that one clinician would supervise thousands of A.I. therapists.

“It is a moral issue to get this out into the hands of people who can’t access care,” said the Limbic executive, who holds a doctorate in computational neuroscience. He added: “We have to remind ourselves: What are we comparing this against? We’re comparing it against no treatment, a long wait list.”

Another medical A.I. pilot with about $60 million in funding is moving forward at the health department’s Advanced Research Projects Agency. Dr. Haider Warraich, a former F.D.A. official and cardiologist, said the Advocate project is meant to ultimately deploy autonomous A.I. to manage care for heart failure patients, giving them access to a chatbot that can prescribe and manage medications.

Dr. Warraich said the project was inspired by his experience as a cardiologist managing heart failure patients during the Covid pandemic. He said his team had routine phone contact with patients, many of whom were afraid to enter the hospital and catch the virus, and found that patients improved with the regular check-ins.

He said the A.I. effort, put into practice by teams at Stanford and Duke, among other groups, would include remote monitoring or wearable sensors linked to the A.I., which could adjust medications if a patient’s condition began to deteriorate. (Given current laws and rules, a doctor will oversee the A.I.)

The goal, he said, “is to really bring safe and effective clinical A.I. to the bedside, and build a regulatory pathway for this technology, so that we can really help unlock the potential of this technology — not just for heart failure, which is our main focus, but really for all conditions.”

Other companies accepted into Medicare’s pilot programs include Slingshot AI and Devoted Health, organizations backed by Andreessen Horowitz, a venture capital firm that has heavily supported Mr. Trump.

Neal Khosla’s company, Curai Health, was selected by Medicare and has an application pending with the F.D.A. to deploy its autonomous A.I. primary care doctors. In a pre-published study by company scientists and engineers, his team found that clinicians concurred with the AI doctor’s diagnosis about 91 percent of the time across about 2,300 cases. However, in three cases, the A.I. suggested a telehealth visit in situations where a human doctor advised an urgent or emergency evaluation.

Given the promise to vastly expand affordable care, the younger Mr. Khosla said he was surprised by the vitriol generated by the recent editorial that he and his father and Dr. Ezekiel Emanuel, a health policy official in the Obama administration, wrote with Abe Baker-Butler in a JAMA journal. The article argued that autonomous A.I. outperformed human doctors in several areas and would be in widespread use by 2030.

Dr. Emanuel said that he got feedback from peers reminding him of the role doctors play in consoling patients. Overall, he said the response has been about “40 percent supportive.”

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

]]>

item.title: 10-Year Treasury Yield Reaches 5%, Highest Level in Years
item.description:
The 10-year Treasury yield, one of the most important interest rates in the world, rose to 5 percent on Monday, its highest level in three years, capping a long stretch of turmoil in the bond market that has pushed up borrowing costs for companies and consumers.

Rates have reached levels that some worry could pose a risk to the economy. The rise in bond yields, which move in the opposite direction to prices, has been fueled by the effects of the war in the Middle East, worries that government spending is out of control and the explosion of spending — and borrowing — by artificial intelligence companies.

The Trump administration has tried to ease Treasury rates by intervening in financial markets, including by aggressively buying back billions of dollars of its bonds. But those efforts have failed to placate bond investors who on Monday pushed yields past 5 percent, as oil prices remained well above $100 a barrel, driving fears of higher inflation.

Last week, President Trump promised to pay $5,000 to every American if the Republicans kept control of Congress in the midterm elections, a proposal that could add $1 trillion to the federal deficit.

The 10-year Treasury yield briefly surpassed 5 percent in October 2023. Before that, the yield had not risen that high since 2007, the year before the global financial crisis.

While the drivers of rising yields then and now are different, the effects are similar. A higher 10-year yield has contributed to rising mortgage rates, with the average 30-year fixed rate mortgage hitting 6.76 percent last week, up from around 6 percent in late February, on the eve of the start of the war in Iran.

Rising rates could also threaten the stock market rally, analysts say, if investors rethink the risk-reward calculation of investing in stocks versus bonds. Higher-yielding bonds offer investors a strong return with fewer risks than stocks. And higher rates can also squeeze corporate earnings, which underpin the stock market, by increasing borrowing costs for companies.

The “greatest near-term concern for stocks,” according to Antony Ghee, head of equity investments for the chief investment office at Merrill and Bank of America Private Bank, is “a sustained push above 5 percent” on the 10-year Treasury yield.

The Trump administration has singled out the 10-year yield as its benchmark for improving everyday affordability for Americans. But that measure has been moving against the White House’s goals this year.

The 10-year yield has risen roughly 0.8 percentage points this year and is more than a third of a percentage point higher than when President Trump returned to office in January 2025. The rise in the 30-year yield has been even steeper, trading at multidecade highs for the past several weeks. The 30-year yield hovered around 5.38 percent on Monday.

Amid the bond turmoil, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has intervened in financial markets in an effort to ease long-term rates.

Last week, the Treasury purchased $5.2 billion of its own debt maturing in the next 10 to 20 years, part of a plan to inject demand into the Treasury market to try to push prices higher and yields lower.

But the Treasury’s purchases fell short of the maximum $6 billion that it had said on Wednesday it could buy, despite receiving more than $10 billion in offers from investors, raising skepticism among some investors about how committed the Treasury was to its plan to reduce yields.

Bond investors are now looking to Federal Reserve to take steps to control inflation. Traders in futures markets now see a 90 percent probability that the Fed raises rates by a quarter of a percentage point at its meeting this week.

There are numerous differences between today’s U.S. economy and that of 2007 when the 10-year Treasury yield peaked around 5.3 percent.

Some investors and analysts note, however, that in both periods a rise in Treasury yields accompanied strong, concentrated growth tied to one industry. Back then it was housing, and now it is A.I.

Technology companies have turned to the debt market to supercharge their growth, borrowing billions to pay for the rapid build-out of data centers and other infrastructure, in turn raising expectations for growth and inflation in the future, which pushes yields higher.

Some analysts have warned that if A.I.’s transformational impact falls short of promises, it could pose a broader threat to the economy.

“The historical analog, whether it is 2007 or any other period of change, is you tend to get excesses before you see it out play out in a more sustainable way,” said Joseph Purtell, a portfolio manager at Neuberger Berman.

Aruni Soni contributed reporting
